newsitem.title: INDIA: INDIA RUPEE - India hitting currency pain barrier.
newsitem.headline: INDIA RUPEE - India hitting currency pain barrier.

text.p: As India moves toward capital account convertibility the country's central bank must decide whether it can pay the price of a rampant rupee.

The Reserve Bank of India bought around $5.0 billion in 1996/97 ended March 31 and around $2.0 billion in the first two months of this fiscal year to try and halt the rupee surfing higher on a wave of foreign capital inflows.
But bigger waves are on the horizon as India moves further toward convertibility, and managing the consequent increase in broad money supply will become an acute problem, analysts said.

"The big danger is on the rupee. Already we are seeing more and more pressure on it. The RBI has to make a big policy decision on what kind of currency it wants," said Nupur Joshi, economist at Jardine Fleming (India) Broking Ltd.
Exporters have already hit the pain barrier.

The rate of export growth in April went into fast reverse, clocking a negative 10.8 percent compared with a positive 13.7 percent in April last year, according to data from the Federation of Indian Export Organisations.
Exporters say the trend began in 1996/97 when export growth slumped to four percent from 21.4 percent the year before.
"India faces a very well defined problem," Mark McFarland, economist with Peregrine Brokerage Ltd in Hong Kong said.
"It exports low value-added products to the world market, and their competitiveness is very much tied to the exchange rate. Allowing the currency to appreciate will only make it worse."
South Asian neighbours' currencies have all fallen against the dollar in the past year, to add to Indian exporters' woes.
India is losing market share for high value basmati rice to Pakistan, tea to Sri Lanka, and jute and garments to Bangladesh, warned one banker.
The Pakistan rupee has fallen around 15 percent against the dollar over the past 12 months, and the Sri Lankan rupee is down 5.5 percent on a year ago.
Meantime the Indian rupee has stayed stubbornly strong against a dollar which has surged against other international currencies, making the rupee's trade weighted performance even stronger.
The rupee was trading at around 35.82 to the dollar on Thursday, virtually unchanged from a year ago.
The lack of diversity in India's export sector increased the vulnerability of the trade performance, analysts said.
Anindya Chatterjee, economist at NatWest Markets in Bombay, believed official expectations of 15-20 percent growth in exports this fiscal year were overblown.
"India's exports, which are non-oil and non-electronics are not going to grow by more than eight percent in 1997/98," Chatterjee said. At the same time imports will head higher.

That spells some hard work lowering India's debt service ratio from 25 percent to 20 percent, after successfully whittling it down from 35 percent when the country embarked on its liberalisation programme in 1991.
Aggressive central bank intervention has helped build India's foreign exchange reserves to their highest levels ever, at $28.22 billion in early June compared to $21.62 billion a year ago.

But the RBI has to face a stark choice on whether to let the rupee firm, when its strength is already damaging exports, or miss its monetary target of 15.0-15.5 percent for M3. Data for late May showed M3 growing at 16.4 percent.
The worst case scenario would be a rising rupee and rising inflation, setting the scene for a future currency shock.

Under the timetable proposed by an expert committee earlier this month, India will relax barriers on outflows of funds before lifting the boom on inflows to try to offset the impact of the incoming funds on the monetary base.

So far the RBI has neutralised the monetary impact of extra rupees in circulation from forex intervention by selling government paper to take the rupees out of the system. But this so-called "sterilisation" is only a short term answer.
